summary:
Liberia criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. The offence of sodomy carries up to one year of imprisonment, applies to women as well as men, and is a domestic-origin provision rather than a colonial import, so no external legal framework presses toward repeal.

There is no legal gender recognition. No administrative route exists for a trans person to amend the name or gender marker on a Liberian identity document, so a visitor whose papers do not match their presentation cannot bring them into consistency before travel or during the stay.

Transition-related medical care is not available domestically. Gender-affirming hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgery are not offered in Liberia, so a visitor who depends on regular hormone supply or post-operative follow-up has no in-country clinical fallback and must arrive with what they need.

The legislative environment is actively hostile. On 16 October 2024, representative Johnson N. Williams was reported to be canvassing other lawmakers for support for a harsh anti-homosexuality bill filed that summer, with related proposals that would imprison children as young as ten years old for gay sex.

Political leadership has publicly defended the criminal law. In March 2012 then-President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf defended the laws criminalising homosexuality in a joint interview, remarks that drew international comment on Liberia's position.

Enforcement of the sodomy law is uncommon, but its existence deters LGBTQ crime victims from reporting to police, and some LGBTQ people have been arrested on the basis of their sexuality or gender identity after attackers used that status as an excuse for the assault. The practical effect is that the statute shapes encounters with the police even where prosecutions are rare.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised. In 2012 then-Senator Jewel Howard Taylor introduced a bill that would have made same-sex marriage a first-degree felony carrying up to ten years; it passed the Senate but not the House, and Sirleaf had threatened to veto either anti-LGBTQ bill put to her that year.

One statutory protection does exist. Section 2.4(b)(iii) of the Decent Work Act 2015 entitles all who seek to work in Liberia to do so regardless of sex, gender identity or sexual orientation, a non-discrimination guarantee that sits alongside, and does not displace, the criminal offence.
tangentialFactors:
The current statute sits within a longer record of legislative pressure. Reporting from April 2012 described anti-gay sentiment growing after another government announced plans to promote LGBT rights overseas, alongside proposed legislation carrying longer jail terms for homosexuality and a distribution of fliers targeting gay-rights supporters; the 2024 bill canvassed by Johnson N. Williams is the most recent instance of that pattern.

The then-president's March 2012 remarks, given in a joint interview in Monrovia, drew international comment on Liberia's stance, with the interviewer declining to comment on his own government's position. The episode indicates that the country's approach to consensual same-sex conduct has been a subject of diplomatic attention rather than purely domestic debate.

Structured documentation of the environment dates from the UNDP and OHCHR country report 'SOGIR in Africa: Liberia', published in April 2020, a participatory review of the legal, social and human-rights conditions for people of diverse sexual orientation and gender identity. Findings published after that date rest on journalistic and advocacy sources rather than on a fresh UN review.

A trans visitor should weigh the employment guarantee against the criminal offence rather than treat them as offsetting. The Decent Work Act 2015 protects access to work on grounds including gender identity and sexual orientation, while the same conduct remains a criminal offence punishable by a year of imprisonment.
localsOnly:
Private spaces where LGBTQ Liberians can be open about their identities do exist, often sponsored by advocacy organisations such as Stop AIDS in Liberia (SAIL) or the Transgender Network of Liberia (TNOL), and in some cases created by private individuals. Outside them, LGBTQ Liberians commonly conceal their identities in public.

Stop AIDS in Liberia, the first NGO founded by LGBTQ Liberians for LGBTQ people, was established to educate men who have sex with men about HIV/AIDS, test them and counsel those testing positive, and expanded its services to all LGBTQ people from 2012.

Health indicators bear on that service environment: a 2013 UN-AIDS survey put HIV/AIDS prevalence among Liberian men who have sex with men at 19.8%, against a backdrop in which transition-related care is unavailable.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the 2024 anti-homosexuality bill is unresolved in these sources: the reporting establishes that a representative was seeking co-sponsors on 16 October 2024, but no source states whether the bill was introduced, referred to committee or passed. Its ten-year minimum for children aged ten and above is described as a related proposal rather than enacted law.

No source in this inventory addresses entry or border screening: whether immigration officers at Roberts International or Ganta entry points inspect gender markers, question trans arrivals, or apply any discretionary refusal power is not sourced here, and the assessment above rests on domestic law rather than on documented border practice.

The absence of legal gender recognition is stated as an absence of any available process; no Liberian statute text or administrative regulation expressly prohibiting amendment of identity documents is cited in these sources, so the finding rests on documentation of a missing route rather than on a quoted refusal provision.

Enforcement frequency is characterised as uncommon by country coverage, with no case-level data, prosecution counts or sentencing record supplied. Whether the Decent Work Act 2015 non-discrimination clause has been invoked or applied in a gender-identity complaint is likewise not sourced, so its practical weight for a resident or visitor is unverified.
